`Rceattle` is integrated with the [`dsem`](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=dsem) package via the `dsem` argument to `fit_mod()`. A dynamic structural equation model (DSEM) lets you place explicit structural relationships on recruitment deviations — including links to environmental covariates and cross-species linkages — instead of treating them as independent random effects.

> **Requires `dsem` 3.0.0.** DSEM models call `dsem::dsem()` internally, and the bundled C++ (`src/TMB/dsem.hpp`) is matched to `dsem` version 3.0.0. Other versions emit an incompatible data layout, so `fit_mod()` stops with an error if a different `dsem` is installed. Install the matching version with `remotes::install_version("dsem", "3.0.0")`.

This vignette covers:

- Specifying a SEM with `build_DSEM()`
- Linking environmental covariates to recruitment in a single-species model
- Linking recruitment across species in a multi-species model
- Inspecting the fitted DSEM object

## `build_DSEM()` arguments

`build_DSEM()` produces the list of DSEM settings consumed by `fit_mod()`. Its main arguments:

- `sem` — text specification of the SEM. One row per link with the form `from -> to, lag, param_name, start_value` (or `<->` for a variance/covariance term). Every variable is either a column of `data_list$env_data` or one of the **latent process columns** the SEM supplies to the population model (see *Which processes a SEM can drive* below). If no start value is given, that term is **not** estimated. The default (when `sem = NULL`) is IID recruitment deviates.
- `family` — measurement-error family for each **env-data variable** in the SEM: `"fixed"` (default; measured exactly), `"normal"`, `"gamma"`, `"bernoulli"`, `"poisson"`, `"lognormal"`, or `"tweedie"`. A single string is recycled across the env variables. The latent process columns are never observed, so they are always `fixed` regardless of this setting. Note that under `dsem` 3.0.0 a non-`"fixed"` family **estimates** that variable's observation-error SD; use `"fixed"` to treat a covariate as measured exactly.
- `sigmaR_prior_sd` — log-scale SD of an optional lognormal prior on each species' estimated recruitment SD, centred on the assessment's own `data_list$sigma_rec`. Default `NA` is no prior. In practice this is the argument that decides whether a real model converges: when environmental covariates over-explain the deviations, the recruitment SD collapses toward zero, and a value of 0.5–1 regularizes it while still estimating it. All four of the production DSEM scripts set it.
- `estimate_projection` — if `FALSE` (default), latent states for the projection period are turned off, simplifying estimation.
- `bound_sd` — whether the sem's standard-deviation paths (`x <-> x`) get a lower bound of 0. `TRUE` by default. Their sign is not identified, so the surface is symmetric about 0: harmless for an MLE, fatal for MCMC. See "Sampling a DSEM" below. Set `FALSE` only to reproduce a fit made before the bound existed, or to demonstrate the symmetry.
- `constant_variance` — what a `<->` term means once the SEM has lagged paths. `"conditional"` (the default, and `dsem`'s) reads it as a disturbance variance; `"marginal"` and `"diagonal"` hold the marginal variance constant instead. All three are identical for a SEM with no lags. See "Which variance a `<->` term means" below.

See `?build_DSEM` and `dsem::make_dsem_ram` for full details on the SEM grammar.

## Setup

```{r}
library(Rceattle)
library(dplyr)
```

## Single-species: GOA pollock

We start with single-species GOA pollock and add a bottom-temperature covariate to `env_data`. Scaling the covariate makes the SEM coefficients comparable across links.

```{r}
data("GOApollock")
GOApollock$projyr <- 2020   # Shorten projection horizon for quicker estimation
GOApollock$env_data <- GOApollock$env_data %>%
  dplyr::mutate(ScaledBT = scale(BTempC))
```

### Model 1: IID recruitment (no DSEM)

With `dsem = NULL`, recruitment deviations are treated as IID random effects — the standard `Rceattle` behaviour.

```{r}
model1 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(
  data_list    = GOApollock,
  inits        = NULL,
  file         = NULL,
  estimateMode = 0,
  random_rec   = TRUE,
  msmMode      = 0,
  initMode     = 2,
  fit_control  = fit_control(phase = FALSE, verbose = 1))

summary(model1)
```

### Model 2: bottom temperature → recruitment

The SEM below specifies (i) a one-year AR(1) process for scaled bottom temperature, (ii) a one-year-lagged effect of temperature on recruitment, and (iii) the recruitment-deviation variance. Phasing (`fit_control(phase = TRUE)`) helps the model reach a sensible starting point before the SEM parameters are turned on.

```{r}
sem_iid <- "
  # link, lag, param_name, start_value

  # internal data relation
  ScaledBT -> ScaledBT,  1, AR_BT,    0
  ScaledBT -> recdevs1,  1, BT_to_R,  0
  recdevs1 <-> recdevs1, 0, sigmaR1,  1
"

model2 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(
  data_list    = GOApollock,
  inits        = NULL,
  file         = NULL,
  estimateMode = 0,
  dsem         = build_DSEM(sem    = sem_iid,
                            family = "fixed"),
  random_rec   = TRUE,
  msmMode      = 0,
  initMode     = 2,
  fit_control  = fit_control(phase = TRUE, verbose = 1))

summary(model2)
```

### Screen the specification before fitting

`fit_mod()` does not check a SEM for you. `check_dsem_spec()` runs the cheap
Tier-1 checks against the built objects and the model's `env_data`, and is worth
a call before committing to a long fit:

```{r}
gp   <- clean_data(GOApollock)
spec <- build_DSEM(sem = sem_iid, family = "fixed")
check_dsem_spec(gp, build_dsem_objects(spec, data_list = gp))
```

It reports predictors observed in only a few hindcast years (a sparse latent can
absorb recruitment variance and drive `sigmaR` to zero), a collinear lag-aligned
design, covariates spanning orders of magnitude in SD, and a variable with no
exogenous variance of its own. That last one is the quiet failure: a variable
whose two-headed path is pinned at zero is computed rather than estimated, so the
`env_data` series supplied for it is never read.

### Compare the two fits

**Do not compare these two by AIC or by `-log L`.** A DSEM's likelihood also scores the covariate's own process — the `ScaledBT -> ScaledBT` AR(1) row — which `model1` does not carry at all, so the two objectives are computed over different data. Measured on this model, `model1` reports `-logL` 742.8 and `model2` 797.9, which makes the environment-linked fit look 55 units worse when it is simply scoring more. To compare, fit an *environment-free SEM* as the baseline — the same AR(1) rows, no path into `recdevs1` — so both likelihoods cover the same quantities. That is what the "IID sem" in the production scripts is for.

```{r}
mod_list  <- list(model1, model2)
mod_names <- c("Single-species IID", "Single-species + BT")

plot_biomass(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names)
plot_recruitment(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names)
```

### Inspect the DSEM object

The fitted model carries the underlying `dsem` object, which can be queried for SEM structure and parameter estimates.

`summary()` on the fitted model prints the SEM path coefficients with standard errors, z-values and Wald p-values, and the per-species recruitment SD. Every path in the sem appears; one the model held fixed — a start-valued path, or the recruitment SD under `random_rec = FALSE` — carries its held value and no standard error.

```{r}
s <- summary(model2)
knitr::kable(s$coefficients)
knitr::kable(s$recruitment_sd)
```

Two cautions when quoting the table. A two-headed (`<->`) row is a variance parameter whose sign is not identified — the model uses its absolute value — so a negative `Estimate` there is not meaningful; compare magnitudes. And its `z_value` / `p_value` test against a boundary of the parameter space, so the usual Wald reading does not apply and they are typically extreme regardless of evidence.

The underlying `dsem` object is on the model as `model2$dsem`, and the specification as `model2$data_list$dsem_settings$sem`.

That object is classed `c("Rceattle_dsem", "dsem")`, so `summary()` on it returns the path table `fit_mod()` recorded — the same numbers as `summary(model2)$dsem_coefficients` — and `plot()` draws the dsem package's path diagram at the estimated coefficients. Use `edge_label = "value"` to label the arrows with them, or `"value_and_stars"` to add significance stars; both need the suggested `dsem` package installed. The two cautions above apply to the figure as well, and are easier to miss there: a `<->` variance whose estimate landed on the negative branch is drawn with a minus sign the model did not use, and its stars test a boundary rather than evidence.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
summary(model2$dsem)
plot(model2$dsem, edge_label = "value")
```

The subclass matters: `dsem::dsem()` classes its own return `"dsem"`, and the object Rceattle carries was built *before* fitting, so the dsem package's own methods would read the starting values and report a converged path as `0`. For the same reason `logLik()`, `vcov()`, `residuals()`, `predict()` and `simulate()` on `model2$dsem` refuse rather than answer — the SEM is one term in a joint CEATTLE objective, not a model fitted on its own, and each refusal names what to use instead (`vcov(model2)`, `process_residuals()`, `sim_mod()`, and so on).

## Which processes a SEM can drive

A latent column name says which process it drives and for which species — and,
for a two-sex species, which sex. A one-sex species carries no sex token, which
is the convention the rest of the package follows.

| latent column | drives | units |
|---|---|---|
| `recdevs<sp>` | recruitment deviations | log scale |
| `l1devs<sp>` | `L1`, mean length at the growth anchor age | cm |
| `linfdevs<sp>` | `Linf`, asymptotic mean length | cm |
| `richdevs<sp>` | the Richards shape parameter `m` | — |
| `mdevs<sp>` | `M1`, residual natural mortality | log scale |

So `l1devs1` is species 1's `L1` in a one-sex model, and `l1devs2f` /
`l1devs2m` are the female and male `L1` of species 2 in a two-sex model.

The growth latents are log-scale multipliers applied through
`growth_linkage_offset`, the same tensor a fixed environmental growth linkage
writes to, so the two **compose**: the covariate carries the explained part and
the latent the residual. They are bias-corrected on the GMRF's marginal
variance, which makes the mean parameter unbiased rather than the median —
mean weight-at-age is the weight in SSB and B40%.

Name a recruitment column for **every** species to have the SEM drive
recruitment, or **none** of them to leave recruitment on its own density. Naming
only some species is an error, and so is a sem that names no latent column at
all: it would contribute a density to the objective while driving nothing.

Growth `K` is **not** drivable. The Jan-1 growth recursion reads the previous
year's K, so a terminal-year K latent reaches a hindcast observation only
through the within-year advance, whose factor is exactly zero at a Jan-1 fleet
and spawning month — perturbing it there leaves the objective bit-identical.
`L1` and `Linf` carry terminal-year information at any timing, so a field on
them has no unidentified final year. A year-varying K is still available as a
fixed or random-effect **growth linkage**
(`build_growth(linkages = list(K = linkage_spec(~ (1 | Year))))`), which is a
separate univariate density rather than part of the SEM's joint field.

A growth latent is refused where the species' growth model never reads that
parameter: any of them under empirical weight-at-age, and `richdevs` under von
Bertalanffy, whose `m` is mapped out. It is also refused beside a **random**
growth linkage on the same parameter, which would be a second random field on
it, each scored by its own density; a fixed linkage composes with it.

### Natural mortality

`mdevs<sp>` is a log-scale multiplier on residual natural mortality `M1`,
applied through `M_linkage_offset` and composing with a fixed environmental M
linkage in the same way the growth latents do. It is **flat over ages**: one
value per species, sex and year, saying that mortality was high or low for the
whole stock that year. Nothing writes it into predation mortality `M2`, but
under `msmMode > 0` M2 moves with it anyway: M1 sets survivorship, survivorship
sets the average numbers predators eat from, and M2 is predator demand over
available prey. On `BS2017MS` a +0.5 spike on one species' latent moved that
species' own M2 by 1.5% and the other two species' by 3.1% and 4.3%.

The correction that makes mean `M1` unbiased does not make mean survivorship
unbiased — `exp(-M)` is convex, so SB0 and B40% keep a Jensen bias, and because
the latent is flat over ages a per-recruit quantity is exposed to it roughly
`nages`-fold. For a 10-age stock with M = 0.2, a plus group and unit maturity and
weight, mean SPR0 over the latent's distribution sits 3.7% above its value with
no latent at sigma 0.2, and 26% above it at sigma 0.5.

**A lagged path into an `mdevs` column is not flagged, and carries a further
trap.** The correction is applied per year, and a lagged path makes the marginal
variance grow along the series, so the subtraction imposes a deterministic trend
on M even with every latent state at zero. On `GOA2018SS` a random-walk M latent
moved terminal-year M1 from 0.200 to 0.086 and SPR0 from 1.23 to 8.17. Nothing
warns, because the effect is smooth in rho: on the same stock, with every latent
state at zero, SPR0 sits 5.5% above its no-latent value under an unlagged latent
and 6.0% above it at rho 0.3, so no threshold separates them. Use an unlagged
latent, or `fit_control(bias_adjust_proc = 0)`. `inst/dev/TRAPS.md` has the full
table.

`M1_re` estimates its own mortality deviations, on its own univariate density,
and they describe the same parameter as the latent — so a sem that names an M
latent for a species whose `M1_re` is on is refused; pick one. `M1_re` modes 2
and 5 vary by year alone, which is this latent's shape exactly, and 3 and 6 vary
by age and year, which contains it; modes 1 and 4 are age-only, and are refused
as well because a flat annual multiplier beside an age-only deviation is a
configuration nobody has shown identified.

A **random** `M1` linkage is refused for the same reason and more directly: it is
a second year-varying field on the same `M1`, each scored by its own density. That matters because `data_check()` steers you from `M1_re` towards the
linkage grammar, so it is the path you arrive on. A **fixed** M linkage composes
with the latent and is not refused.

## Multi-species: EBS three-species model

`recdevsN` indexes the recruitment deviations of species `N`. In a multi-species model, this lets you link recruitment processes across species — e.g. the recruitment of one species predicting the recruitment of another in the same year.

```{r}
data("BS2017SS")
BS2017SS$projyr <- 2020
```

### Model 3: three-species IID recruitment

```{r}
model3 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(
  data_list    = BS2017SS,
  inits        = NULL,
  file         = NULL,
  estimateMode = 0,
  random_rec   = TRUE,
  msmMode      = 0,
  fit_control  = fit_control(phase = TRUE, verbose = 1))

summary(model3)
```

### Model 4: cod and ATF recruitment → pollock recruitment

Species in `BS2017SS` are ordered pollock (1), Pacific cod (2), arrowtooth flounder (3). The SEM below keeps each species' own variance and adds two same-year cross-species links into pollock recruitment.

```{r}
sem_3spp <- "
  # link, lag, param_name, start_value
  recdevs1 <-> recdevs1, 0, sigmaR1,  1
  recdevs2 <-> recdevs2, 0, sigmaR2,  1
  recdevs3 <-> recdevs3, 0, sigmaR3,  1
  recdevs2 -> recdevs1, 0, R2_to_R1, 0
  recdevs3 -> recdevs1, 0, R3_to_R1, 0
"

model4 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(
  data_list    = BS2017SS,
  inits        = NULL,
  file         = NULL,
  estimateMode = 0,
  random_rec   = TRUE,
  dsem         = build_DSEM(sem    = sem_3spp,
                            family = "fixed"),
  msmMode      = 0,
  fit_control  = fit_control(phase = TRUE, verbose = 1))

summary(model4)
```

### Compare the two fits

```{r}
mod_list  <- list(model3, model4)
mod_names <- c("Three-species IID", "Three-species linked")

plot_biomass(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names)
plot_recruitment(Rceattle = mod_list, model_names = mod_names)
```

## Diagnostics on a DSEM fit

Every diagnostic in `vignette("model-diagnostics")` runs on a DSEM fit, and that vignette has a section saying which of them mean something slightly different. The short version: OSA residuals cover the assessment data exactly as without a DSEM (the covariate series is not among them, and under `family = "fixed"` it carries no measurement density to residualize); recruitment process residuals are whitened by the process precision rather than divided by a per-year SD; `profile(param = "sigmaR")` resolves to the SEM's variance path; and `self_test(process = TRUE)` re-realizes the SEM rather than drawing IID deviations, handing back the drawn field in `attr(sims, "process_sim")$dsem_x_tj`. A covariate declared with a measurement family is simulated too — its state with the field, its observation from the family that scores it, written back into `env_data`. `run_mse()` is the one thing that still refuses.

## Sampling a DSEM

The two-headed `<->` self paths are diagonals of a Cholesky factor, so the likelihood sees only their squares and their sign is not identified. That costs nothing at the MLE — there are simply two mirrored optima — but it makes the posterior bimodal by construction, so an unconstrained sampler either sits in whichever mode it started in or wanders between them, and R-hat and any credible interval on σ are meaningless.

`build_bounds()` bounds those diagonals at 0, which is the standard identifying restriction for a Cholesky factor and rules out nothing the likelihood could distinguish. Pass the same bounds to the sampler:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# fit$bounds$par_lower / $par_upper are aligned to fit$obj$par -- that alignment
# is done inside fit_mod(), against obj$par's own block order. Do not build the
# vector by indexing fit$bounds$lower (a list keyed by parameter block) with
# names(fit$obj$par): that repeats whole blocks and returns a vector far too
# long. tmbstan expands a vector of this length across the random effects itself.
post <- tmbstan::tmbstan(fit$obj,
                         lower = fit$bounds$par_lower,
                         upper = fit$bounds$par_upper)
```

`build_DSEM(bound_sd = FALSE)` turns the bound off, and with it the sign flip `fit_mod()` otherwise applies to a negative starting value. That is what to use if you want to reproduce a fit made before the bound existed parameter for parameter, or to show for yourself that the two optima are mirrored — the objective is identical at `+sigma` and `-sigma`.

A variable that also carries a cross-covariance (`A <-> B`) or a lagged two-headed path keeps unbounded support: its row of the factor has off-diagonal entries, so identifying the sign means flipping the whole row rather than the one element. `fit_mod()` names those variables when it builds the bounds, and their marginals will show the same mirroring until you identify them another way — a prior, or a reparameterization outside the SEM.

## Which variance a `<->` term means

This only matters once your SEM has a **lagged** path. With simultaneous effects only, the three `constant_variance` settings are mathematically identical, and on the bundled GOA pollock model they return the same objective to every printed digit.

`dsem` inherits RAM notation from the `sem` package, and in the structural-equation tradition a `<->` self-loop is the **disturbance** (innovation) variance — the residual, conditional on the incoming paths. That is `dsem`'s default and Rceattle keeps it. The consequence is that the *marginal* variance of the process grows along the causal graph. For a first-order self-path with correlation ρ it is σ²/(1−ρ²), so it climbs steeply as ρ approaches 1:

| ρ | marginal variance | implied 95% recruitment range |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | σ² | 50× |
| 0.5 | 1.33 σ² | 130× |
| 0.7 | 1.96 σ² | 640× |
| 0.9 | 5.26 σ² | 8,700× |

Two things follow, and neither is a bug — they are what the convention means:

- **The lognormal bias correction uses the marginal variance**, which is correct: `rec_dev = z − bias_adjust_proc · margvar/2` is what makes `E[exp(rec_dev)] = 1`. `margvar` is reported as `quantities$dsem_margvar_tj`, so you can read it. It is *not* `R_sd²` once the SEM is lagged.
- **`sigmaR_prior_sd` centres on `data_list$sigma_rec`**, which is the assessment's marginal recruitment SD. Under `"conditional"` the prior therefore lands on the innovation SD. The two coincide for an IID SEM and diverge by 1/(1−ρ²) once you add a self-path, so check that the prior is still saying what you meant.

`constant_variance = "marginal"` rescales `Gamma` and `(I − Rho)` so the marginal variance stays constant, which makes the `<->` term the marginal SD. That is the time-series convention, and it is what `ar1(1 | Year)` already uses elsewhere in Rceattle, and what WHAM's `Ecov` AR(1) and `glmmTMB`'s `ar1()` use. Measured on a SEM with ρ = 0.6, the ratio of marginal variance to `R_sd²` is 1.5625 under `"conditional"` — exactly 1/(1−0.6²) — and 1.0000 under `"marginal"`.

Rceattle keeps `dsem`'s default rather than picking a side, because a `<->` term is a disturbance variance in the notation the SEM is written in. If you want the time-series reading, ask for it:

```{r}
build_DSEM(sem = sem, family = "fixed", constant_variance = "marginal")
```

Bear in mind that changes what the estimated recruitment SD means, so a value fitted under one setting is not comparable to one fitted under the other.

## Writing the SEM

One row per link, `from -> to, lag, param_name, start_value`, with `<->` for a variance or covariance term. Comments start with `#` and blank lines are ignored, so a specification can be laid out to read:

```{r}
sem <- "
  # source        link   target       lag   parameter    start
  ScaledBT   ->   ScaledBT,      1,   AR_BT,       0
  ScaledBT   ->   recdevs1,      1,   BT_to_R,     0
  recdevs1  <->   recdevs1,      0,   sigmaR1,     1
"
```

Aligning the columns like this is fine — `build_dsem_objects()` normalizes the spacing around every arrow before the SEM reaches `dsem`. (It did not always: `dsem` 3.0.0 compares path strings literally when deciding whether a variable already has a variance, so a padded `<->` used to make it add a second one and take the R session down with it.)

Each variable takes exactly **one** variance term. Leave the line out entirely and `dsem` adds a freely estimated one; write it with a start value to estimate it from there; write it twice and `build_dsem_objects()` says so.

## Tips

- **Phasing.** DSEM-linked models can be sensitive to starting values. Setting `fit_control(phase = TRUE)` fits the assessment in stages and typically reaches a better starting point before the SEM parameters are turned on.
- **Estimating vs. fixing parameters.** Any SEM term written *without* a `start_value` is treated as fixed and is not estimated. Provide a start value to estimate the term.
- **Projections.** Latent DSEM states are not estimated for projection years by default. Set `estimate_projection = TRUE` if you need them — this adds parameters and can complicate estimation.
